m6-t1.introduction: A second way to understand “Product concept & market validation”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Turn an idea into a testable problem
sections.explanation: A problem statement identifies a specific user, job and current workaround before proposing a feature.

items.label: Specific user
items.detail: Name a group you can actually reach with permission.

items.label: Job and pain
items.detail: Describe the task and its observed difficulty.

items.label: Current alternative
items.detail: Find out how the work is done today.

items.label: Testable claim
items.detail: State what evidence would support or weaken the problem.

sections.takeaway: A broad technology idea is not evidence that someone needs the product.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Ask about behaviour, not polite approval
sections.explanation: Past events and real workarounds are more informative than asking whether someone likes your idea.

items.label: Ask about the last time
items.detail: Get a concrete event and its steps.

items.label: Explore the workaround
items.detail: Ask what was tried and what it cost in effort.

items.label: Listen without pitching
items.detail: Avoid leading the person toward your preferred answer.

items.label: Synthesize faithfully
items.detail: Keep quotations and interpretations distinct.

sections.takeaway: Record permission, source and limitations; interview notes are not permission for unrestricted AI upload.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. User interviews that tell the truth

sections.title: The alternative may not be another app
sections.explanation: A phone call, notebook or manual routine may be trusted and effective. Compare it honestly with the proposed change.

items.label: Current routine
items.detail: Identify what users rely on and why.

items.label: Its strengths
items.detail: Understand trust, accessibility and low switching effort.

items.label: Its limits
items.detail: Find observed gaps rather than invented competitor weaknesses.

items.label: Switching burden
items.detail: Include time, learning, access and risk in the comparison.

sections.takeaway: Do not call an alternative ineffective merely because it uses less technology.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A persona panel produces questions, not customers
sections.explanation: Synthetic objections can help you prepare research. They are not observations from real users.

items.label: Present known facts
items.detail: Give the panel the same bounded problem statement.

items.label: Collect objections
items.detail: Ask for different concerns about value, cost and harm.

items.label: Convert to questions
items.detail: Identify the missing evidence behind each objection.

items.label: Investigate for real
items.detail: Use permitted interviews, observations or source checks.

sections.takeaway: Label the rehearsal and take important objections back to real evidence.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A lean canvas is a set of hypotheses
sections.explanation: The canvas connects user, problem, value, solution, reach, economics and measures. Its contents should change when evidence changes.

items.label: People and problem
items.detail: State the target users, need and current alternatives.

items.label: Value and solution
items.detail: Describe the benefit and smallest plausible response.

items.label: Reach and relationships
items.detail: Explain how users would encounter and trust it.

items.label: Economics
items.detail: Record cost and revenue assumptions without invented results.

items.label: Measures and evidence
items.detail: Name the tests that would support or reject the assumptions.

sections.takeaway: Do not present assumptions in a canvas as validated market facts.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Make the first version small enough to learn
sections.explanation: A narrow MVP tests a specific uncertainty. Manual steps can be valid when they are disclosed honestly.

items.label: One user and job
items.detail: Limit the audience and problem for the first test.

items.label: One usable channel
items.detail: Choose a delivery path the users can access.

items.label: Visible assumptions
items.detail: Disclose manual work and unfinished automation.

items.label: Measured learning
items.detail: Collect the planned evidence and decide what to change.

sections.takeaway: Define success and a decision date before seeing the result.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A team charter makes contribution reviewable
sections.explanation: People need shared expectations about decisions, work and credit before the build becomes busy.

items.label: Roles
items.detail: Name responsibilities and how they can rotate.

items.label: Working rhythm
items.detail: Set communication, review and disagreement rules.

items.label: Done means
items.detail: Agree what evidence makes a task complete.

items.label: Contribution log
items.detail: Keep attributed decisions and work records.

sections.takeaway: Record actual contributions rather than inventing a symmetrical team story at submission.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can a synthetic persona panel replace required user interviews?
checkpoint.answer: No. It can suggest questions but cannot provide genuine user behaviour, consent or validation evidence.

m6-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “Build sprint: app, AI feature & data”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Scope the sprint around what tests the idea
sections.explanation: A backlog should protect the smallest complete learning experience from expanding into an unfinished feature collection.

items.label: State the user story
items.detail: Connect an action to a specific user benefit.

items.label: Identify the Musts
items.detail: Keep only work necessary for the core test.

items.label: Define done
items.detail: Name observable behaviour and the evidence to check it.

items.label: Defer deliberately
items.detail: Record what will not be built this sprint.

sections.takeaway: A feature is not “done” merely because its screen exists.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. Scoping: the backlog and the definition of done

sections.title: Architecture is a map of data and authority
sections.explanation: Inputs, records, AI steps, automation and interfaces must fit together with explicit access and ownership.

items.label: Input
items.detail: Collect the minimum permitted information.

items.label: Data store
items.detail: Keep validated records with ownership and access rules.

items.label: AI feature
items.detail: Perform a narrow, checked transformation.

items.label: Automation
items.detail: Move work with clear triggers and safeguards.

items.label: Interface
items.detail: Show states and actions appropriate for the user.

sections.takeaway: Every connector expands the data-flow review; more integrations are not automatically better.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: An AI feature needs an enforced boundary
sections.explanation: A prompt specification is only one control. Validate the output and test failure behaviour before users rely on it.

items.label: Specify
items.detail: Name inputs, output fields, allowed values and unknown states.

items.label: Test offline
items.detail: Try typical, malformed and boundary cases with expected results.

items.label: Validate in the flow
items.detail: Reject unsupported values and malformed structure outside the model.

items.label: Approve and monitor
items.detail: Keep human checks, a review queue and an owner.

sections.takeaway: A high pass count on a small sample does not justify ignoring an unacceptable safety failure.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: The build log is the report’s source of truth
sections.explanation: Daily evidence makes changes and contributions traceable. It prevents the final report from becoming a polished reconstruction.

items.label: Record work
items.detail: Name who did what and link the artefact.

items.label: Record decisions
items.detail: Explain the evidence and trade-off behind a choice.

items.label: Record failures
items.detail: Keep blockers, tests and corrections visible.

items.label: Use the log
items.detail: Write the report from records, not memory or invented figures.

sections.takeaway: Do not turn plans, estimates or test scenarios into claims of completed live results.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A sprint rhythm should preserve a working path
sections.explanation: Short reviews expose blocked work early and make simplification possible before the final demonstration.

items.label: Check in
items.detail: Share progress, next work and blockers briefly.

items.label: Demonstrate
items.detail: Show the current end-to-end flow early.

items.label: Simplify
items.detail: Reduce scope when a task is not converging.

items.label: Retest
items.detail: Keep the core path usable after each addition.

sections.takeaway: An honest manual pilot step is preferable to a concealed broken integration.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: AI contributions still need a named reviewer
sections.explanation: Planning, drafting and critique can accelerate work, but a person remains responsible for artefacts that enter the product.

items.label: Request bounded help
items.detail: Use permitted material for a specific task.

items.label: Inspect the suggestion
items.detail: Check correctness, safety and fit with the build.

items.label: Test before accepting
items.detail: Run the relevant checks on the actual artefact.

items.label: Credit and own it
items.detail: Name the assistance and the responsible team member.

sections.takeaway: Keep confidential data out of unapproved tools and log who checked each accepted contribution.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 6. Using AI as a team member (properly)

checkpoint.question: Does a prompt that passed nineteen of twenty sample tests establish that a product is safe for every use?
checkpoint.answer: No. It is limited sample evidence. Inspect the failed case, block unacceptable outputs and test integration, permissions, language and recovery for the actual use.

m6-t3.introduction: A second way to understand “Integration, testing, privacy & go-live”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Integration means testing every hand-off
sections.explanation: A working block can fail when another system supplies a different format, identity, time or permission.

items.label: Agree formats
items.detail: Define dates, units, IDs and language codes.

items.label: Match authority
items.detail: Check each account’s permitted reads, writes and actions.

items.label: Coordinate timing
items.detail: Use explicit time zones and dependencies.

items.label: Test the whole flow
items.detail: Run fresh, duplicate and failure cases end to end.

sections.takeaway: Test duplicate runs and least-privilege access as well as the normal happy path.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. Integration: making the blocks one thing

sections.title: A test plan asks several different questions
sections.explanation: Functional success is only one part of readiness. Quality, recovery, privacy and usability need their own evidence.

items.label: Functional
items.detail: Does each required task satisfy its definition of done?

items.label: AI quality
items.detail: Are content, language, structure and boundaries acceptable?

items.label: Failure
items.detail: What happens when inputs, quotas or dependencies fail?

items.label: Privacy and security
items.detail: Are data and actions restricted to authorised roles?

items.label: Usability
items.detail: Can the intended users understand and complete the task?

sections.takeaway: Write expected results first and retain failures and fixes, not only the final green summary.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Graceful failure needs detection and ownership
sections.explanation: A fallback is useful when it tells the truth, prevents unsafe action and gives the user a recoverable next step.

items.label: Detect
items.detail: Validate the input or receive a clear error signal.

items.label: Contain
items.detail: Stop unsafe actions and preserve the pending work.

items.label: Explain
items.detail: Tell the user what happened without exposing private internals.

items.label: Recover
items.detail: Use a bounded retry or an owned review queue.

sections.takeaway: Do not silently invent missing values or retry an outward action without limits.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. Failure handling users can live with

sections.title: A privacy notice must describe the actual workflow
sections.explanation: A notice and data checklist are practical safeguards, not a standalone legal compliance certificate. Requirements depend on the real context.

items.label: Map data
items.detail: List collection, processing, recipients and storage.

items.label: Minimise
items.detail: Remove fields unnecessary for the purpose.

items.label: Explain choices
items.detail: Describe the actual use, retention and contact route clearly.

items.label: Verify controls
items.detail: Check permissions, deletion and withdrawal procedures where applicable.

sections.takeaway: Review current official requirements and institutional policy with an authorised owner; do not assume a template is sufficient.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. Privacy notice and pre-launch data checklist

sections.title: External text must not acquire tool authority
sections.explanation: A user message or retrieved page can contain instructions that try to redirect a model. Prompt formatting alone cannot enforce a secure boundary.

items.label: Receive untrusted content
items.detail: Treat forms, documents and messages as data.

items.label: Limit capabilities
items.detail: Give the feature only the access its task needs.

items.label: Validate results
items.detail: Check structure and evidence before using the response.

items.label: Approve effects
items.detail: Require the appropriate person before an irreversible or external action.

sections.takeaway: Keep validation, least-privilege tools and human approval outside the model’s say-so.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Release is a reviewed decision, not a working demo
sections.explanation: A pilot begins only when the planned controls, support and measurement are actually ready for its audience.

items.label: Review evidence
items.detail: Inspect tests, language quality and resolved exceptions.

items.label: Check safeguards
items.detail: Verify access, notice, monitoring and the kill switch.

items.label: Assign operations
items.detail: Name support hours, review queue owner and feedback route.

items.label: Run the bounded pilot
items.detail: Use the agreed scope, measures and review date.

sections.takeaway: An unchecked privacy or safety item is a reason to pause even if the core feature runs.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 6. The launch checklist and the pilot

checkpoint.question: Is quoting external text inside delimiters enough to prevent prompt injection?
checkpoint.answer: No. Delimiters help structure content but are not a security boundary. Enforce permissions, validate outputs and protect consequential actions with independent controls.

m6-t4.introduction: A second way to understand “User insights, growth planning & the pitch”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Pilot feedback combines behaviour and explanation
sections.explanation: Usage signals, conversations and observation answer different questions. Together they help distinguish activity from value.

items.label: In-product signal
items.detail: Collect a low-effort response under a clear privacy rule.

items.label: Short conversation
items.detail: Ask what helped, confused or changed for the user.

items.label: Observation
items.detail: Watch what people actually do, with permission.

items.label: Evidence log
items.detail: Keep dates, provenance, themes and subsequent actions.

sections.takeaway: Do not treat positive comments or repeated opens as proof of the intended outcome.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. Feedback loops that fit a pilot

sections.title: Reach, engagement, outcome and quality differ
sections.explanation: An enrolled user, a repeated interaction and a changed real task are not the same unit of success.

items.label: Reach
items.detail: Count who was eligible or enrolled and who left.

items.label: Engagement
items.detail: Define the actual use event over a stated period.

items.label: Outcome
items.detail: Measure the specific user task the product aims to improve.

items.label: Quality
items.detail: Track checked AI output and harmful or failed cases.

sections.takeaway: Show denominators and measurement limits; a small pilot is not a causal proof of business impact.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Ship a change you can evaluate
sections.explanation: Feedback themes should remain tied to actual records. A revision needs a hypothesis and a repeatable check.

items.label: Group actual feedback
items.detail: Keep counts and representative quotations traceable.

items.label: Choose a problem
items.detail: Prioritise a meaningful issue with manageable effort.

items.label: Make one change
items.detail: Record what changed and what should improve.

items.label: Measure and review
items.detail: Check the intended outcome and possible side effects.

sections.takeaway: Do not invent themes or treat a favourable before/after difference as proof of cause.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Persevere, pivot and stop are legitimate decisions
sections.explanation: The purpose of a pilot is to learn whether the proposed use deserves more effort. Continuing is not automatically the successful answer.

items.label: Persevere
items.detail: Continue a supported direction with visible remaining risks.

items.label: Pivot
items.detail: Change the user, job or approach in response to evidence.

items.label: Stop
items.detail: Retire an unsupported or unsafe direction and preserve the learning.

sections.takeaway: State what evidence supports the decision and what would change it.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A pitch is an evidence narrative
sections.explanation: The audience needs the user’s problem, a working demonstration, measured learning and a defensible next decision.

items.label: Problem and people
items.detail: Show the specific need and its evidence.

items.label: Product and demo
items.detail: Explain the core flow and show it working or failing gracefully.

items.label: Pilot and responsibility
items.detail: Trace results, safeguards and changes to records.

items.label: Decision and ask
items.detail: State what you learned and the appropriate next step.

sections.takeaway: Keep the demonstration’s failure path and limitations visible rather than hiding them behind polished slides.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A case study should be reproducible after the pitch
sections.explanation: The report connects the problem, design, tests, results and individual contribution to an evidence pack.

items.label: Collect records
items.detail: Use the build log, test log and measurement sheet.

items.label: Trace each claim
items.detail: Link the headline statement to the supporting artefact.

items.label: Describe contribution
items.detail: Separate your work, team work and AI assistance.

items.label: Publish safely
items.detail: Remove restricted data and retain limitations in the public version.

sections.takeaway: Keep all figures consistent across report, slides and portfolio; label simulated work honestly.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 6. The capstone report and the portfolio

checkpoint.question: Is stopping a pilot necessarily a failed capstone decision?
checkpoint.answer: No. An evidence-based stop or pivot can demonstrate good judgement. Explain the findings, safety limits and what you learned without inventing success.

items.label: Purpose

items.label: Build an artefact
items.detail: Create the required work for the stated audience and scope.

items.label: Verify and explain

items.label: Two-page report

items.label: Working product and backup

items.label: Five-minute pitch

items.label: Evidence pack

items.label: Individual reflection

items.label: AI-use disclosure

sections.title: Check the boundaries before the build or release
sections.explanation: A good-looking artefact cannot compensate for missing permission, invented evidence or an unsafe action.

items.label: Evidence and scope
items.detail: Use the required real or clearly labelled practice evidence honestly.

items.label: Permission and rights
items.detail: Check relevant data, likeness, music and source permissions.

items.label: Human control
items.detail: Keep the required review before consequential outward effects.

items.label: Test and disclose
items.detail: Record actual results, limitations and AI assistance.

sections.takeaway: Follow the topic-specific constraints in full; a disclosure label does not override the rules.

items.label: Week 8 · build

sections.title: Make the published criteria inspectable
sections.explanation: The original rubric, weights, pass threshold and any caps remain authoritative. These panels point to the evidence behind its criteria.

items.label: Problem and validation
items.detail: Support the specific user need with actual research.

items.label: Working product
items.detail: Show an end-to-end useful flow with tested fallback.

items.label: Pilot and iteration
items.detail: Trace observations, feedback and a genuine revision.

items.label: Responsible build

items.label: Pitch and report

items.label: Team contribution

sections.title: Prepare for evidence questions, not only a demo
sections.explanation: A reviewer needs to understand value, boundaries and recovery as well as what appears on screen.

items.label: Who is the user?
items.detail: Identify the specific people and observed need.

items.label: What changed?
items.detail: Trace the reported benefit to actual evidence.

items.label: What is refused?

items.label: Who owns failure and data?
items.detail: Show recovery, operational ownership and authorised handling.

sections.title: Use the review habits, not a success formula
sections.explanation: The original tips are practical prompts for reflection, not guarantees of a result or new assessment conditions.

items.label: Narrow or stop honestly
items.detail: A changed idea can demonstrate learning when the evidence justifies it.

items.label: Disclose manual steps
items.detail: A permitted manual pilot is not a fully automated product.

items.label: Show graceful failure

sections.title: Separate tool help from your responsibility
sections.explanation: A useful statement tells the reviewer where assistance entered and what the learner independently checked.

items.label: Name the assistance
items.detail: Identify tools and the tasks for which they were used.

items.label: Trace the evidence
items.detail: State which real sources, tests and outputs were checked.

items.label: Own the judgement
items.detail: Describe selection, revisions, decisions and individual or team contributions.

items.label: Follow the policy
items.detail: Keep assessment restrictions and rights boundaries intact.

sections.takeaway: Disclosure cannot legitimise fabricated evidence, prohibited tool use or missing permission.

checkpoint.question: If the pilot could not run, may you invent a plausible usage table?
checkpoint.answer: No. Follow the original documented-reason and usability-test alternative, state what actually happened and preserve the limitation. Never fabricate a pilot or consent.
